exercises.question: White to move. In a Sicilian (1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e6 5.Nc3 Qc7 6.Be2), Black has just developed with 6...Bd6?. Win material.
exercises.explanation: Look at every knight jump: 7.Ndb5! attacks the queen on c7 and the bishop on d6 at the same time, and nothing can take the knight on b5. If the queen moves, for example 7...Qb8, then 8.Nxd6+ wins the bishop with check. Black's best try, 7...Bxh2, gives up the queen after 8.Nxc7+ Bxc7 for a knight and a pawn. 7.Ncb5 makes the same fork and also wins material, but it is less precise: 7...Qa5+ escapes with check.

wrong.why: A normal developing move; Black can play ...a6 and the fork is gone.
Safe, but it lets Black untangle with ...a6 or ...Be5; the fork was available now.

exercises.hint: Which knight jump attacks the queen and the bishop at the same time?
exercises.objective: Review: spot a knight fork of queen and bishop by checking every knight jump.

exercises.question: Black to move. White's king is far away, but the b-pawn is running. Which move saves the game?
exercises.explanation: Draw the square of the b4-pawn: b4-b8-f8-f4. Only Kf4 steps into it, and from there the king catches the pawn: 1...Kf4 2.b5 Ke5 3.b6 Kd6 4.b7 Kc7. The white king on h8 is far too slow to help. Kf3, Kg4 and every other move leave the black king one tempo short.

wrong.why: The third rank is outside the square: 2.b5 and the pawn queens.
The g-file is outside the square; 2.b5 Kf5 3.b6 Ke6 4.b7 and Black is one move late.

exercises.objective: Review the rule of the square in a race against a passed pawn.

exercises.question: White to move. You are a bishop up. Black's queen offers a trade. What is the safest winning move?
exercises.explanation: When you are a piece up, trading queens removes your opponent's only real counterplay. 1.Qxd5 exd5 leaves a simple bishop-up ending that White wins by bringing the king to the centre. The queen trade also solves the back-rank problem: as long as queens are on, Black's queen is eyeing d1.

wrong.why: Moving the queen off the d-file allows 1...Qd1#; White's back rank is weak.

exercises.hint: What is Black's only active piece?
exercises.objective: Convert a material advantage by trading queens and removing counterplay.

exercises.question: Black to move. White's queen and bishop aim at h7. Find a good defensive move.
exercises.explanation: White threatens Qxh7#. Nf6 defends h7 and attacks the queen at the same time, so White loses a tempo. ...g6 (blocking and hitting the queen) is equally good. What matters is that you name the threat before playing your own plan: the natural ...cxd4 or ...c4 is met by Qxh7#.

wrong.why: Continues the plan and ignores the threat: 2.Qxh7#.
Attacks the bishop, but 2.Qxh7# comes first.

exercises.hint: What does White threaten on h7?
exercises.objective: Spot a mate threat before continuing your own plan, and defend with tempo.

exercises.question: White to move. Black's queen guards the back rank. Find mate in two.
exercises.explanation: The black queen is overloaded: it must both protect the rook on d8 and keep the back rank closed. 1.Qxd8+! forces 1...Qxd8, and 2.Rxd8# mates because the king on g8 is boxed in by its own pawns. Any quiet move lets Black trade rooks on d1 and the chance is gone.

wrong.why: 1...Rxd1+ 2.Qxd1 and the back-rank pressure has disappeared.
Threatens nothing serious; 1...g6 or ...Rxd1+ and Black is fine.

exercises.hint: Forcing moves first: what happens after the biggest capture?
exercises.objective: Calculate a forcing two-move sequence against an overloaded defender.

exercises.question: Black to move. Your pawn is still on e7. Which move wins?
exercises.explanation: Lead with the king and take the opposition: after 1...Ke6 the kings face each other with White to move, and the black king will reach a key square in front of the pawn (1...Ke6 2.Kf4 Kd5 or 2.Kd4 Kf5). The pawn on e7 still has spare tempo moves for later opposition battles. Pushing the pawn first, or putting the king beside it, lets White blockade.

wrong.why: 2.Kd4 takes the opposition; with the king beside the pawn Black cannot make progress.
Walks away from the pawn: 2.Ke5 and the white king blockades in front of it.

exercises.hint: King in front of the pawn, and make the opponent move.
exercises.objective: Review: win king and pawn against king with the opposition and spare pawn tempi.

exercises.question: White to move. In the Symmetrical Four Knights (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4 5.O-O O-O 6.d3 d6 7.Bg5) Black played 7...g6?. Your bishop pins the knight on f6 to the queen. Calculate, and play the strongest move.
exercises.explanation: 8.Nd5! attacks the pinned knight a second time and also hits the bishop on b4. Calculate Black's replies. If the pinned knight takes, 8...Nxd5 9.Bxd8 Nxd8 10.exd5, White has won the queen for a bishop. If the bishop on b4 moves away, for example 8...Bc5, then 9.Bxf6 Qxf6 10.Nxf6+ wins a piece with check. A pin is worth most when you can attack the pinned piece again before the opponent can break it.

wrong.why: Useful in general, but it gives Black time for ...Bxc3 and ...Qe7, and you win much less.
It damages Black's pawns but does nothing to the pinned knight; Black regroups.

exercises.hint: Which move attacks the pinned knight a second time and something else as well?
exercises.objective: Calculate the opponent's best replies to find out whether a pin really holds.

exercises.question: Black to move. In the Smith-Morra Gambit (1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.Nf3 e6 6.Bc4 Qc7 7.O-O Nf6 8.Qe2 Ng4), White has just attacked your knight with 9.h3. Retreating looks forced. Calculate the alternatives and play the best move.
exercises.explanation: Before retreating, look at forcing moves. 9...Nd4! attacks the queen on e2 and sets up ...Qh2#, because your queen on c7 and the knight on g4 both aim at h2, and only the knight on f3 defends it. If 10.Nxd4?? then 10...Qh2# is mate. White's best is 10.hxg4 Nxe2+ 11.Bxe2, and Black has won the queen for a knight. This is the Siberian Trap.

wrong.why: A safe retreat, but you miss the chance to win the queen.
It trades a pair of knights and you stay a pawn down; Nd4 wins the queen.

exercises.hint: Can you attack the queen in a way that makes capturing your knight fatal?
exercises.objective: Calculate forcing moves before retreating an attacked piece: a counter-threat can be bigger than the threat.

exercises.question: White to move. Win the c6-pawn and the game.
exercises.explanation: White's king wants d6 or b6, but the direct approach meets the opposition. Kf5! outflanks: after 1...Ke7 2.Ke5 Black must give way, and after 1...Kd7 2.Kf6 the king heads for e7-d6. The c5-pawn controls d6 and b6, so the black king can only defend from d7 or c7 and runs out of squares.

wrong.why: 1...Ke7 takes the opposition and White cannot get past.
1...Kd7 and the black king holds the c6-pawn; draw.

exercises.hint: Approach from the side, not head-on.
exercises.objective: Review outflanking in a blocked king and pawn ending.

exercises.question: Black to move. Should you trade rooks? Play the best move.
exercises.explanation: Calculate the pawn ending: after 1...Rxe1 2.Kxe1 Black has an outside passed h-pawn. It drags the white king to the kingside while the black king marches to the queenside pawns. With rooks on, White's rook stops the h-pawn and the game is roughly equal.

wrong.why: Keeps rooks; 2.Rh1 and the white rook holds the h-pawn back.
A check that leads nowhere: 2.Kc1 and White's rook still guards the kingside.

exercises.hint: Which pawn ending would you reach, and who wins it?
exercises.objective: Simplify into a pawn ending only after calculating that the outside passed pawn decides.

exercises.question: White to move. Black threatens Qb2#. Which move saves the game?
exercises.explanation: Look at your own king first: it has no legal move, and the a2-pawn is blocked. If your rook disappears, it is stalemate. 1.Rf8+! Kxf8 is forced (h8 and f7 are covered by the rook) and White has no legal move. Any normal move loses to ...Qb2#.

wrong.why: Covers b2 for a moment, but 1...Qc3+ 2.Rb2 Qxb2# mates anyway.
1...Qxc1+ and Black wins easily.

exercises.hint: Your king cannot move. Can you make your rook vanish?
exercises.objective: Review the stalemate resource: sacrifice your last piece when your king has no moves.

exercises.question: Black to move. White has a dark-squared bishop and an a-pawn. Find the only move that draws.
exercises.explanation: The a-pawn queens on a8, a light square, and White's bishop is dark-squared, so it can never drive a king out of a8. Black must get to the corner at once: 1...Kd5 2.Kd3 Kc6 3.Kd4 Kb7 and the king reaches a8. Moves to the kingside are one step too slow.

wrong.why: Runs the wrong way: 2.a5 and the pawn cannot be caught.
2.a5 Ke6 3.a6 and the pawn queens.

exercises.hint: Which corner can the bishop never control?
exercises.objective: Review the wrong-coloured bishop fortress and reach the corner in time.

exercises.question: White to move. The c7-pawn is one step from queening. Find mate in two.
exercises.explanation: Black's rook has two jobs: stop the c-pawn and guard the back rank. 1.Rd8+! deflects it: after 1...Rxd8 2.cxd8=Q# the new queen mates on the back rank. Slower moves still win, but checks first would have found the immediate mate.

wrong.why: Strong, but not mate: Black defends with ...Rf8 and the game goes on.
Calm, but it lets Black organise ...Kf8 and ...Ke7.

exercises.objective: Use a deflecting check to promote with mate.

exercises.question: Black to move. You are behind in material. Find the move that turns the game around.
exercises.explanation: White's queen and king stand on the same open file. 1...Rhe8! pins the queen to the king; it cannot leave the e-file, and 2.Qxe8+ Kxe8 gives Black a queen for a rook. Every other move leaves Black simply behind.

wrong.why: Offers a trade but misses the pin; after 2.O-O White stays a piece up.
Defends f7 passively; 2.Qf4+ and White is still a knight ahead.

exercises.objective: Review: spot a pin of the queen against the king.

exercises.question: White to move. Find the only winning move.
exercises.explanation: The black king is on b7, defending c6 from the queenside. Ke5! heads for d6 by the side door: if 1...Kc7 2.Ke6 and 3.Kd6 wins the pawn, and if 1...Kc8 2.Kd6. The black king cannot cover both d7 and d6 because the c5-pawn takes d6 and b6 away from it. Kc4 or Kd3 waste the moment and Black regroups with ...Kc7.

wrong.why: 1...Kc7 and the black king is back in front of the pawn; draw.
Too slow: 1...Ka6! and the black king attacks c5 in time; it is a draw.

exercises.hint: Head for d6 by the shortest route that avoids the opposition.
exercises.objective: Calculate the king route in a blocked pawn ending.
